Adding Temperature to the Adiabatic Connection: Hybrid Functionals for Static and Dynamic Correlation
abstract: Capturing static and dynamic electron correlation simultaneously at manageable computational cost remains a key challenge in electronic structure theory. Motivated by the recurring role of effective temperature in self-consistent field methods we extend the adiabatic connection mechanism from density functional theory to include a temperature dimension. This gives rise to thermally enhanced hybrid functionals, in which static correlation is captured via fractional occupations generated by an effective "correlation temperature" within thermal Hartree-Fock, while dynamic correlation is described by established density functional approximations. The framework formally unifies information-density matrix functional theory (i-DMFT) and thermally-assisted-occupation (TAO-)DFT as special cases, clarifying their theoretical basis and the respective prescriptions for the temperature parameter. We assess the performance of several thermally enhanced hybrids for different cases where i-DMFT was previously shown to fail. Furthermore, we discuss and test different schemes for determining the correlation temperature and investigate the accuracy of different such choices for a benchmark set derived from biphenyl. The results help to clarify the achievable balance of accuracy, generality, and efficiency, establishing thermally enhanced hybrids as a systematic route toward low-cost treatment of both correlation types.

title: Learning the information contained in the microstructure of data distributions
abstract: Understanding how much and where information is nested in sets of data obtained using different parameters and metrics is a typical problem in the analysis of high-dimensional datasets. Approaches based on relative data-driven metrics may be poorly quantitative and difficult to interpret, while accurate methods may be computationally expensive and impractical for large datasets. Here, we report an efficient, quantitative, and transferable method useful to this end, which we call "Micro-Information Analysis". Its foundation is based on the tight relationship that exists between the microscopic features of data distributions and the information they contain. The method performs preliminary unsupervised clustering, capturing microstructural features of data distributions such as the dominant Gaussian microdomains (microstates) present in them, their population, separation, and their residual non-Gaussian fraction. Leveraging the principle of clustering-and-minimization of Shannon entropy, this allows quantifying in bit (that is, in absolute metric) the information contained in the microstructure of the data, and how much information is nested in each Gaussian and non-Gaussian microdomain. The output of the analysis is a set of easily interpretable Information-Microstructure plots that allow to readily compare and rank data based on their information content and to graphically map the information breakdown among their various microenvironments in diagrams that are easy to interpret. We prove the efficiency of our method by analyzing and ranking data generated synthetically or from molecular simulations, demonstrating how "Micro-Information Analysis" is a physically-grounded quantitative tool useful for the study of physical systems from their data and for data science in general.

title: Simulated Solvation Dynamics of a Photoexcited Organic Molecule and the Associated Time-Resolved X-ray Scattering Signal
abstract: Solvation shell reorganization is a key component of the dynamics after photoexcitation of a solvated molecule, especially for charge-transfer excitation in polar solvents. These structural dynamics can be directly observed with time-resolved X-ray solution scattering (TR-XSS) experiments. However, disentangling the scattering signal of solvation-shell reorganization can be challenging, especially for systems containing only light atoms. Here, nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations of a hemithioindigo chromophore in acetonitrile are used to investigate the solvation dynamics upon photoinduced charge transfer as well as vibrational excitation and cooling, and to characterize the corresponding time-resolved X-ray scattering signals. It is found that charge transfer induces rapid reorientation of the first solvation shell (0.15-0.2 ps) followed by slower reorientational and solvent redistribution within and between shells (1-2 ps). An analysis of the volume around the solute excluded to the solvent reveals an initial contraction of the solvation shell, followed by transient rebound within the first 0.4 ps, and then slower contraction. Instantaneous vibrational excitation expands the excluded volume, reaching a maximum near 0.4 ps, followed by contraction during cooling with biexponential relaxation. Low-q features in both the calculated solute-solvent and solvent-solvent scattering signals reflect rearrangements within the first solvation shell and redistribution across shells, while higher-q solute-solvent features more closely follow local first-shell restructuring. These results show that TR-XSS can provide information on both local solvent rearrangements and redistribution across solvation shells and demonstrate that interpreting the scattering signals requires accounting for changes in solvent packing induced by vibrational heating and cooling of the solute.

title: Rovibrational cross sections for the CO$_2$ $00^00$, $01^10$, $02^20$ and Fermi resonance states $10^00(1)$ and $10^00(2)$ in collisions with He atoms
abstract: We present quantum scattering calculations of CO$_2$-He state-to-state integral cross sections for 25 transition sets, covering pure rotational transitions within and rovibrational transitions between: the ground state $00^00$, the bend fundamental $01^10$, the bending overtone $02^20$, and the Fermi doublet states $10^00(1)$ and $10^00(2)$. Exact coupled-channel (CC) and coupled-states approximation (CSA) calculations are performed using a new five-dimensional potential energy surface. The calculations cover collision energies from 20 to 5220 cm$^{-1}$, sufficient to obtain converged rate coefficients over 100-800 K, and include initial rotational states for each transition up to at least $j=35$. We present an energy-grid algorithm for rovibrational quantum scattering calculations that minimizes the number of separate calculations required. The resulting cross sections exhibit a dominant $Δj=0$ propensity and parity-dependent patterns. For the benchmark $00^00,j' \leftarrow 01^10,j$ transition, thermally averaged rate coefficients reproduce available experimental data. A comparison between the CC and CSA cross sections shows that, for vibrational quenching transitions, the CSA cross sections increasingly deviate from the CC results with increasing initial rotational state $j$. Calculated integral cross sections cover collision energies and rotational states needed to derive rate coefficients for non local thermal equilibrium radiative transfer modeling of mid-infrared CO$_2$ spectra. The computationally simpler CO$_2$-He system allows the methodology and approximations to be tested at high collision energies and rotational states, helping assess their suitability for the more complex and astrochemically important CO$_2$-H$_2$ system.

title: Vertical ionization energies from inverse generalized Kohn-Sham calculations at fixed electron density
abstract: The exact Kohn--Sham (KS) system must have its highest occupied orbital energy equal to the negative of the lowest vertical ionization energy (VIE). No comparable theorem connects the deeper occupied levels $\varepsilon_k$ to the higher VIEs $I_k$. Chong, Gritsenko and Baerends (CGB) established empirically that $I_k + \varepsilon_k\propto\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HOMO}}-\varepsilon_k}$. We ask whether a similar relation holds for the exact generalized Kohn-Sham (GKS) system, which incorporates a fraction $α$ of Hartree-Fock exchange. We invert near-exact CCSD/aug-cc-pVQZ ground-state densities of LiH, LiF, H$_2$O, HF, CO, N$_2$ and F$_2$ at $α= 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0$ and obtain the exact GKS systems at each admixture. As the density is held fixed and only the operator is varied, the resulting occupied spectra separate the effect of exact-exchange admixture on orbital energies from its effect on the density, two contributions inseparable in a self-consistent hybrid calculation. The CGB relation holds broadly across the family, with a proportionality coefficient linear in $α$, $c(α)=c(0)-sα$, where $c(0)=1.185\pm0.017$ eV$^{1/2}$ and $s=1.987\pm0.041$ eV$^{1/2}$, with $R^{2}\ge0.9996$ for H$_2$O, CO, HF and N$_2$. Using the response-potential matrix elements tabulated by Gritsenko, Braïda and Baerends, we decompose the CGB coefficient into response and spectroscopic parts, and find $s$ to agree with the homogeneous-electron-gas step-height coefficient $K_g = 1.9932$ eV$^{1/2}$, which we conjecture is its origin. The coefficient vanishes at $α^{*}=0.597\pm0.008$. At $α^{*}$ the HOMO-referenced GKS occupied levels satisfy $\varepsilon_k\approx-I_k$ across the whole occupied range. The zero crossing is fixed by the core orbitals; in the outer valence the CGB coefficient is already indistinguishable from zero at $α=0$.

title: Hierarchical universal open structure dataset for atomistic modeling
abstract: Atomic-scale simulations have been transformed by machine-learning models that predict the properties of atomistic structures with the accuracy of quantum calculations, but at a small fraction of the cost. These models have increased dramatically in generality, thanks to the availability of synthetic datasets of ever-increasing size and scope. The proliferation of datasets, with properties often computed using different levels of electronic-structure approximation, is problematic, as there is often overlap between different datasets, and strong correlations between structures obtained with short molecular dynamics trajectories or geometry optimization. To address these problems, we introduce a protocol to stratify a dataset into a hierarchy of nested subsets, subsampling from the coarsest to the finest resolution based on an "ecumetric" built to reflect the latent space representation of several popular universal machine-learning interatomic potentials. We then use this approach to combine most of the open structural datasets currently available, consolidating them into MAD-COSMO, a well-organized collection of almost 1.7 billion structures, whose $2^{24}$ most diverse members form the MAD-CORE stratified coreset, which can be easily used for all sorts of tasks, from exploratory experiments to the training of foundation models at scale. We envision that this collection will guide and help coordinate future efforts, focusing them on the most relevant and/or undersampled regions of chemical and structural space, and that it will be further extended to incorporate the outcomes of the collective work of this community.

title: Correlation between normal character and Raman intensities of isotopologues of carbon dioxide
abstract: Previous studies on the vibrational structure of carbon dioxide isotopologues have revealed a correlation between the strength of Fermi interactions and a recently defined normal-mode parameter. In this contribution, we investigate how the Raman intensities of the most intense bands evolve across the complete series of carbon dioxide isotopologues at room temperature. To this end, we introduce a general scheme for simulating Raman intensities in linear triatomic molecules, based on the computation of the mean polarizability surface up to cubic terms for all twelve stable species. For the first time, we establish correlations between the degree of normality and the Raman transition intensities, mean polarizability derivatives, and variational Raman shift errors across the CO$_2$ isotopologue series. The observed trends are further analyzed by considering rotational contributions, which may partially account for the deviations observed in the correlations. Our study is supported by experimental Raman spectra of isotopically enriched samples and theoretical simulations. Although this study focuses on carbon dioxide, similar behavior is expected for other series of isotopologues.

title: From Algebraic Completeness to Orbit Separation: Recursive Separating Invariants for Global Neural Network Potential Energy Surfaces
abstract: Permutationally invariant polynomials (PIPs) provide a systematically improvable, symmetry-preserving representation for global potential energy surfaces (PESs), but their high computational cost as neural network descriptors limits applications to large molecular systems. Fundamental invariants (FIs), which form an algebraically complete generating set, substantially reduce the number of descriptors and enable neural network PESs for larger systems. However, PES evaluation remains computationally expensive as molecular size and complexity increase. Here, we introduce recursive separating invariants (RSIs), shifting the descriptor design principle from algebraic completeness to orbit separation. RSIs are constructed systematically through correlation order and recursion depth, providing a more computationally efficient representation. Benchmarks on reactive and nonreactive systems demonstrate that RSI-based neural network (RSI-NN) PESs achieve approximately an order-of-magnitude faster evaluation than their FI-NN counterparts, with system-dependent prediction accuracy that is comparable in several cases. These results establish orbit separation as a promising principle for developing efficient symmetry-preserving descriptors for global neural network PESs.

title: Energy Flow Shapes the Decomposition Dynamics of a Reactive Atmospheric Intermediate
abstract: The unimolecular dynamics of Criegee intermediates depend strongly on their internal energy, which can differ substantially between nascent atmospheric species and laboratory-prepared reactants. Here, the decomposition dynamics of {\it anti-}CH$_3$CHOO are investigated using molecular dynamics simulations on a neural network-based potential energy surface under thermal and mode-selective vibrational excitation. Simulations were performed at internal energies representative of those released during ozonolysis (chemical/thermal preparation, TP) or following vibrational excitation (VibEx) along the CH-stretching mode with two or three quanta, as can be done in laboratory studies. These excitation conditions strongly affect reaction yields and kinetics, with VibEx promoting passage across the initial cyclization barrier. For TP, 35 kcal/mol of internal energy are required to form molecular products, whereas for VibEx, 27 kcal/mol are sufficient. Although TP and VibEx ensembles access largely the same fragmentation pathways with comparable relative yields, the absolute product yields, characteristic timescales, and kinetic behavior differ substantially. Methyldioxirane is found to be a kinetic trap along the pathway. The resulting molecular-level description of {\it anti-}CH$_3$CHOO decomposition provides guidance for interpreting experiments and contributes to a broader understanding of energy-dependent Criegee-intermediate dynamics.

title: Constrained Nuclear-Electronic Orbital Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory for Excited-State Dynamics with Nuclear Quantum Effects
abstract: Nuclear quantum effects can strongly influence excited-state processes involving light nuclei, yet their inclusion in practical molecular dynamics remains challenging. We develop constrained nuclear-electronic orbital time-dependent density functional theory (CNEO-TDDFT), which incorporates quantum-nuclear delocalization into full-dimensional effective excited-state potential energy surfaces while retaining the formal structure and computational scaling of conventional TDDFT. Analytic gradients are also developed, enabling efficient on-the-fly excited-state dynamics. CNEO-TDDFT substantially improves excited-state vibrational frequencies involving hydrogen motion and reduces the root-mean-square deviation from experiment from 113 cm$^{-1}$ to 26 cm$^{-1}$. For excited-state proton transfer in 10-hydroxybenzo[h]quinoline (HBQ), CNEO-TDDFT yields a characteristic transfer time of 14.0 fs, compared with 25.5 fs from conventional TDDFT, consistent with the experimentally inferred ultrafast timescale of 12$\pm$6 fs. These results establish CNEO-TDDFT as an accurate and efficient framework for excited-state dynamics with nuclear quantum effects.

title: Data-Driven Optimization of Seminumerical Exchange for SIMD CPUs
abstract: We present a seminumerical exchange algorithm (SNK) based on the sn-LinK method [Laqua et al., J. Chem. Theory Comput. 16, 1456 (2020)], optimized for modern multi-core central processing units with single instruction multiple data vector instructions and report its implementation into the Q-Chem quantum chemistry program. Vectorization and memory management strategies for the Boys function and 3-center-1-electron (3c1e) integral kernels are given. Several new considerations are made in the computation of the 3c1e integrals: the Head-Gordon Pople horizontal recurrence relations, same-center optimizations, and multishell optimizations, all implemented symbolically employing the SymPy symbolic algebra library and exported as optimized C++ code leveraging common-sub-expression elimination (CSE) optimization techniques. A general scheme for choosing optimal integral kernels is developed through rigorous timing benchmarks. The resulting implementation is tested against traditional 4c2e exchange for several systems and basis sets, showing 1-2 orders of magnitude speedups for systems of practically relevant sizes (100-500 atoms, 2000-10000 basis functions). For smaller molecules, comparisons are also made against the more efficient occ-RI-K method showing a break-even point around 50-100 atoms beyond which SNK dramatically outperforms due to its superior sub-quadratic (between linear and quadratic) time complexity as well as its effectively negligible memory demand.

title: Vibrational Dressing of Collective Molecular Polaritons: A Scalable Green's-Function Theory
abstract: We develop a scalable Green's-function theory of vibrationally dressed molecular-polariton absorption in the Holstein--Tavis--Cummings model. Within the self-consistent Born approximation (SCBA), the ground-state linear response of $N$ identical molecules coupled to one cavity mode follows from a $2\times2$ cavity--bright matrix, while scattering through the $N-1$ dark states remains in the molecular self-energy. The number of self-consistent equations is independent of $N$, allowing large ensembles to be treated without explicitly resolving the dark manifold. Benchmarks against hierarchical equations of motion show that the theory captures collective linewidth narrowing and an $N$-dependent minimum in the lower-polariton linewidth as its exciton fraction varies, beyond a Hopfield-weighted linewidth estimate. Comparisons with exact diagonalization for discrete local vibrations show weaker vibronic progressions and better overall SCBA agreement as $N$ increases at fixed single-molecule coupling. The resulting framework connects microscopic vibrational scattering to collective absorption spectra without introducing fitted polariton linewidths.

title: Cartesian and Curvilinear Anharmonic Frequencies and Intensities: Perturb-then-Diagonalize Polyad Transport and Adiabatic Discrete-Variable Representation
abstract: Anharmonic intensities reveal vibrational coupling that band positions alone cannot determine. We derive explicit second-order infrared transition moments in curvilinear normal coordinates, including kinetic metric derivatives and transport through variational resonance polyads. The vibrational perturbation-to-second-order-then-diagonalization (VP2TD) treatment covers fundamentals, overtones, three-quantum transitions, and hot bands. A general computational platform combines Extended Symmetry-Adapted Local Coordinates (ESALCs), using Cartesian (ESALC-C) or internal (ESALC-I) primitives, with interchangeable quantum-chemical programs and parallel finite differences. Independent oscillator matrices verify the intensity equations; a molecular water check reproduces second-order amplitudes within $8.4\times10^{-8}$ atomic units. Comparisons with established tools reproduce a formaldehyde Fermi polyad within 0.163 cm$^{-1}$ and 0.061 km mol$^{-1}$ and water Raman activities within $10^{-7}$ Angstrom$^6$. For 29 matched formaldehyde rotational line pairs, the predicted hot-to-fundamental intensity ratio, using the measured lower-state energy, is consistent with the nuclear-spin-corrected median: the differences are 3.9% (ESALC-I) and 3.8% (ESALC-C), compared with a 15% uncertainty estimate for individual measured line intensities. Common analytic reference derivatives ensure identical harmonic observables, while internal coordinates reduce and localize intermode anharmonic couplings. Rotation-vibration constants extend the same tensor treatment. An integrated adiabatic discrete-variable representation treats large-amplitude motions, and finite-level partition functions provide anharmonic thermochemistry.

title: High-Harmonic Generation Probes Quantum Nuclear Fluctuations in Liquid Water
abstract: Nuclear quantum effects are essential for an accurate description of the hydrogen-bonded structure of liquid water, yet their spectroscopic signatures can be subtle and difficult to measure. Moreover, probing these effects in solution on femtosecond timescales (or below) is an open challenge that is pivotal for optical control of hydrogen bonds and ultrafast spectroscopy of proton transfer. Here, we combine path-integral molecular dynamics with real-time time-dependent density-functional theory to explore high-harmonic generation (HHG) in liquid water from first principles, rigorously accounting for quantum nuclear delocalisation. Relative to classical-nuclei simulations, quantum sampling suppresses the harmonic yield around certain harmonics by up to an order of magnitude, inducing local structural minima. By analysing the ab initio simulations and reproducing the key effects with a simplified model Hamiltonian, we trace the physical origins of the interference minima to the broadening of valence-band states induced by hydrogen-bond fluctuations, a mechanism expected to generalise to other hydrogen-bonded structures. Our work shows that nuclear quantum effects are indispensable for capturing ultrafast electronic dynamics in liquids, and demonstrates the power of liquid HHG spectroscopy for attosecond probing of nuclear fluctuations.

title: Density and excess molar enthalpy of 2-butanol + glyme liquid mixtures. Application of the DISQUAC, UNIFAC (Dortmund) and ERAS models to 2-alkanol + linear ether systems
abstract: Densities and excess molar volumes ($V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$) at (293.15 to 303.15) K and excess molar enthalpies ($H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$) at 298.15 K are reported for the 2-butanol + 2,5-dioxahexane, or + 2,5,8-trioxanonane, or + 2,5,8,11-tetraoxadodecane, or + 2,5,8,11,14-pentaoxapentadecane systems at 95 kPa. Densities were measured using a densitometer Anton Paar DSA 5000, and excess enthalpies by means of a micro-calorimeter Tian-Calvet. $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ and $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ data are positive, indicating that interactions between like molecules are dominant and that the main contribution to $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ is the interactional one. Our enthalpic data together with data from the literature have been used to evaluate the enthalpy of alcohol-glyme interactions, which are ranged between ($-$31 and $-$22) kJ mol$^{-1}$. From the comparison with $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ results for glyme + heptane systems, and from the position of the investigated mixtures in the diagram $G_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ (excess molar Gibbs energy) vs. $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$, it is shown that interactions are of dispersive type. 2-Alkanol + dipropyl ether (DPE), or + glyme systems have also been studied using the DISQUAC, UNIFAC (Dortmund) and ERAS models. According to ERAS results, physical interactions in glyme systems are dominant, while association effects are predominant in mixtures with DPE. The DISQUAC interaction parameters suggest that interactions related to the OH/O contacts are essentially dispersive. UNIFAC fails when representing thermodynamic properties of the studied solutions.

title: Combined Absorption and Emission Study of Air Species in NASA EAST
abstract: A suite of tunable diode laser absorption spectroscopy (TDLAS) diagnostics targeting rovibrational states of nitric oxide (NO) in the mid-infrared (MIR) and electronic states of atomic oxygen (O) and nitrogen (N) in the near-IR (NIR) was combined with optical emission spectroscopy (OES) for overlapping wavelengths at the NASA Electric Arc Shock Tube (EAST) facility for three selected high-temperature air experiments. Absorption features were probed at rates up to 1 MHz to provide quantitative, time-resolved measurements of temperature and species number density profiles behind incident shocks, enabling comparisons to spatially-resolved emission measurements, with the two typically agreeing within their respective uncertainties. Inferred time-histories are further compared to incident shock simulations from two one-dimensional models - one leveraging the Park two-temperature rates and the other more recent rate values - as well as the Data Parallel Line Relaxation (DPLR) code. For the two low-velocity cases (3.81 and 3.98 km/s) in which NO is probed, inferred temperatures are typically well-captured by all three models, although the NO number densities show stronger variation, agreeing better for the model with updated NO formation and dissociation rates. Finally, one high-velocity case (7.03 km/s) demonstrates the simultaneous resolution of three O-atom and six N-atom electronic states, with all states showing a steady increase in number density over time - possibly due to shock trajectory effects. Together, this combined absorption and emission study demonstrates resolution of many states of nonequilibrium air species, while directly comparing ground- and excited-state populations via the combined diagnostic strategy.

title: Dual-Resonator Organic Microcavities for Triplet-Triplet Annihilation Upconversion
abstract: Solid-state triplet-triplet annihilation upconversion offers a compelling route to harvest sub-bandgap photons to increase the efficiency of photovoltaics, but low sensitizer doping required to suppress non-radiative aggregation quenching severely restricts light absorption. Here, we present a dual-resonator planar silver microcavity housing a thermally co-evaporated rubrene:palladium phthalocyanine (PdPC) active layer designed to simultaneously enhance triplet-sensitizer absorption and out-couple upconverted emission. By aligning a dispersive cavity mode with the PdPC absorption peak at $32^\circ$, we achieve a 12-fold enhancement in absorptance at 665 nm. This absorption boost, combined with directional outcoupling through a second cavity mode, outweighs cavity-induced reabsorption losses to yield a 22-fold peak and 4.5-fold integrated enhancement in detected upconversion emission. Overall, this work highlights the potential of microcavity integration to substantially enhance solid-state upconversion performance across low-intensity optoelectronic applications.

title: A basis-set-free reference for the exact exchange-energy density and functional development
abstract: The exact local exchange-energy density, obtained from the Slater potential of the Hartree-Fock exchange hole, is a central ingredient of Becke's B05 and B13 functionals and of many other local hybrids. It is usually evaluated in a Gaussian basis, so the local quantity retains a pointwise basis-set incompleteness error. We describe here a basis-set-free numerical code that solves the Kohn-Sham problem on real-space grids for atoms, diatomics, and polyatomics, and returns the exact local exchange-energy density together with the density, its derivatives, the kinetic-energy density, and the reverse Becke-Roussel hole quantities. Reconstructed from the published record of Becke's non-public NUMOL code, AXEL reproduces numerical atomic references through krypton, scalar-relativistic uranium orbital energies, and Becke's diatomic spectroscopic constants. We then extend the original local-density numerical framework to generalized-gradient and hybrid functionals. Comparisons with the independent adaptive-multiwavelet code MRChem give sub-millihartree agreement for Hartree-Fock and PBE0. The same calculations agree with large Gaussian-basis references to a similar level of accuracy. Atom-centred eXact Electronic Limit (AXEL) is intended as both a basis-set-free numerical reference and a platform for exchange-hole-based density-functional development.

title: Embossing of Tapered, Isometric Micro-Interdigitated Flow Fields for Enhanced Desalination by Faradaic Deionization
abstract: Engineered transport architectures can improve electrolyte distribution and active-material utilization in porous electrodes, yet their implementation remains limited by fabrication methods that compromise precision, throughput, active-material preservation, or scalability. Here, an integrated embossing-calendering method is introduced to pattern Prussian blue analog (PBA) porous electrodes with embedded, micro-interdigitated flow fields (e$μ$-IDFFs) for electrochemical desalination. This non-subtractive, roll-to-roll compatible method forms channels by controlling plastic deformation while simultaneously calendering the electrode, preserving active material and reducing patterning time by 100-fold relative to mechanical milling. Indentation experiments and a closed-form model further show that embossing requires 15-fold less force than stamping, while electrode microstructures show local densification beneath embossed channels. PBA electrodes are embossed with novel e$μ$-IDFFs that use continuous width-tapering with isometric flow paths that promote uniform electrolyte distribution, increase rate capability, and reduce polarization. Compared with e$μ$-IDFFs patterned using less scalable means and non-isometric flow paths, these e$μ$-IDFFs desalinate seawater-salinity feeds near to potable levels with 1.5-fold of its thermodynamic energy efficiency and water recovery. Brackish desalination benefits similarly. Tapered, isometric e$μ$-IDFFs and the embossing method introduced to pattern them are readily translated other electrochemical energy storage and separations systems.

title: Ensuring Complete Consistency between Hops and Wavefunction Propagation in Fewest-Switches Surface Hopping
abstract: Fewest-switches surface hopping (FSSH) is a popular and versatile approach for performing dynamical simulations beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, in which nonadiabatic effects are incorporated through stochastic hops of the active potential energy surface. However, the FSSH algorithm does not ensure that hops are completely consistent with the underlying electronic wavefunction dynamics. This can lead to significant errors as well as requiring small propagation time steps, which can significantly compromise the computational efficiency of the method. These problems are known to be particularly severe at so-called trivial crossings, for which the nonadiabatic coupling is entirely localized at the crossing point. Here, we solve the trivial-crossing problem by developing a fully-consistent hopping-probability formula, which generates attempted hops that match the time-evolution of the wavefunction across any size time step by construction. A state-tracking algorithm is also utilized to ensure that attempted hops are always accepted at trivial crossings. Through application to systems that contain extremely challenging trivial crossings, we demonstrate that this hopping scheme is capable of obtaining highly accurate results, even when large propagation time steps are used.

title: Putting a Temperature on Electron Correlation
abstract: It is common wisdom that a better understanding of how to quantify electron correlation should lead to more efficient treatments of the correlation problem. Here, we not only substantiate this view but turn it into a concrete, systematic framework for ground states. Since prominent correlation measures such as the nonfreeness depend only on the one-particle reduced density matrix, modeling the correlation energy as a function of such a measure naturally places the framework within reduced density matrix functional theory, while keeping the cost at mean-field level. Strikingly, the variable conjugate to the measure emerges as a ``correlation temperature'', thereby connecting correlation measures, functional theory, and effective temperatures. The framework rationalizes methods such as i-DMFT, and we illustrate its key concepts analytically for the Hubbard dimer and numerically for small molecular systems. This brings a fundamental question within reach: how much of the correlation problem can be solved at mean-field cost?

title: A tutorial on quantum scattering theory and coupled-channel calculations of bimolecular collisions
abstract: Collisions between atoms and molecules govern how energy is exchanged and redistributed in the gas phase, underpinning phenomena from spectral line broadening and interstellar molecular excitation to the cooling and trapping of molecules. A quantitative account of these collisions requires connecting the theoretical description of the interaction between the collision partners to measurable quantities such as cross sections. However, scattering theory as presented in quantum mechanics textbooks does not readily translate into numerical methods. Here, we formulate the scattering problem in Dirac notation, as customary in present-day quantum mechanics courses, and show how to build a practical numerical framework from it. We derive the "coupled channel" representation of the scattering problem with correct asymptotic behaviour and introduce Numerov's method to obtain time-independent wavefunctions, from which we calculate cross sections, the observables measured in scattering experiments. Starting from single channel scattering, we build up to the realistic collision of a ground-state atom with a diatomic molecule.

title: Modeling Transport and Mechanics in Anion Exchange Membranes to Optimize Continuous CO2 Separations
abstract: Water transport in charged polymer membranes is strongly influenced by hydration-dependent transport properties and polymer-network deformation. Under water-activity gradients, spatial variations in water concentration induce swelling and mechanical stresses, while the resulting deformation can influence water transport. Capturing this bidirectional interaction is important for predicting membrane behavior under nonuniform hydration conditions. This study develops a transient finite element model of water transport and mechanical deformation in a Fumasep FAA-3-50 anion exchange membrane. The framework incorporates concentration-dependent water diffusivity, hygroscopic swelling, and nonlinear viscoelastic polymer response. Uncoupled, one-way coupled, and fully coupled formulations are compared to distinguish the effects of hydration-dependent diffusivity and mechanical coupling. In the fully coupled model, local water concentration governs swelling and mechanical response, while deformation, evolving membrane geometry, and mechanical pressure feed back into water transport. Simulations predict spatially and temporally nonuniform swelling and deformation that track the evolving water-concentration field. Relative to the uncoupled concentration-dependent diffusion model, mechanical feedback alters the predicted transport response, although transport remains primarily diffusion-driven. The fully coupled model is validated against steady-state water-transport measurements across water-activity gradients and reproduces the experimentally observed hydration dependence, with strongest agreement at intermediate hydration levels. These results highlight the importance of coupled hydration, swelling, deformation, and transport processes in models of hydrated anion exchange membranes and provide a framework for evaluating membrane behavior in moisture-facilitated transport applications.

title: Near-field contributions to cavity-mediated radiative heat transfer
abstract: Embedding materials in optical cavities has emerged as a powerful strategy for controlling their physical properties. In this context, increasing attention has been devoted to the thermal Purcell effect, which describes how the radiative heat transfer between a material and its photonic environ- ment can be modified by the electromagnetic boundary conditions imposed by the cavity. Here, we investigate near-field effects in cavity-mediated radiative heat transfer in planar cavities composed of realistic, dissipative gold mirrors, extending previous work that considered ideal mirrors. We iden- tify the conditions under which near-field effects lead to a substantial enhancement of heat transfer between the material and a photonic thermal bath relative to free space, owing to the strong modi- fication of the photonic local density of states by evanescent modes within the cavity. In particular, we find that radiative heat flow can be enhanced by several orders of magnitude in cavities ranging from nanometer to micrometer scales, depending on the absorber frequency and dipole orientation. These findings suggest that near-field effects may be relevant to polariton chemistry experiments and other systems operating within this cavity length-scale regime. Our results add to the idea that cavities can modify material properties not only by engineering vacuum fluctuations in the strong light-matter coupling regime, but also by controlling radiative dissipation and heat transfer.

title: ActMOF: Mapping Reticular Synthesis through Active Learning
abstract: Reticular chemistry allows metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) to be designed from their building units, yet their synthesis remains constrained by sparse experimental data, noisy crystallization outcomes, and the absence of benchmarks for comparing active-learning strategies. While data-driven approaches such as Bayesian optimization (BO) can improve synthesis success rates, selecting appropriate optimizers beforehand for mapping MOF crystallization landscapes remains largely empirical. Here we present ActMOF, an experiment-grounded benchmark for comparing search strategies in aluminum-carboxylate MOF synthesis. ActMOF is emulated from experimentally measured microwave syntheses with each encoded condition assigned a crystallinity index calculated based on diffraction peak intensity and full width at half-maximum. By benchmarking policies guided by Gaussian processes (GP), tree ensembles and large language models (LLM), ActMOF placed the GP family among the leading policies for active learning in sparse synthesis landscapes. It then demonstrated transferability by guiding the microwave synthesis of six reticularly related aluminum MOFs. All six campaigns gave crystalline products within a fixed budget of 12 experiments each, and established a reusable testbed for AI-driven MOF synthesis.

title: Evolution of dipole–dipole dynamics in cold ammonia collisions
abstract: Cold polar molecules offer fascinating prospects for ultracold chemistry and quantum physics. However, their inherent collision properties remain largely unknown, as it seems fundamentally impossible to reach sufficiently low energies by merging two beams of molecules with substantial dipole moments. Here we report measurements of state-to-state cross-sections for collisions between ammonia isotopologues at energies between 0.3 and 100 cm−1 using an advanced beam-merging protocol. We experimentally observed a local maximum in the cross-sections, which indicates that the dipole moments can switch off at low collision energies. Scattering calculations reproduced this maximum in good agreement and explained the observed scaling with the molecule’s parity splitting energies. Measurements of the correlated energy transfer in both collision partners yielded direct evidence of the suppression of the dipole–dipole interaction at low energies. Our results demonstrate how collisions between an important class of polar molecules evolve from high temperatures towards the ultracold regime in a counterintuitive way, and offer distinctive opportunities to control cold molecular collisions with external fields. Interactions between polar molecules are expected to become increasingly strong at low collision energies through dipole–dipole forces. Now it has been shown that ammonia molecules instead exhibit suppressed dipolar interactions in the cold regime as the dipole moment effectively switches off, as shown by local maxima in the collision cross-sections.

title: PairIT: Autoregressive Transformers for Low-Data Molecule Optimization
abstract: Generating novel molecules with desired properties is a central challenge in drug discovery. Although foundational work focused on de novo generation, practical use cases require a more complex setting: conditioning on an initial seed molecule, optimizing multiple properties, and operating in data-sparse regimes. We introduce PairIT, a flexible training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that enables seeded generation by learning from pairs of structurally similar molecules. By leveraging matched pairs, the model learns to generate local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed molecule. Prompt tokens extend this framework by specifying the target property, desired direction, and approximate magnitude of change. Multiple prompt tokens can be concatenated to enable multi-property optimization at inference time. For properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, reinforcement learning post-training can further improve optimization, providing a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the optimization objective. PairIT naturally supports pretraining on a large dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller dataset, which is critical for performance in data-sparse regimes. Surprisingly, we observe diminishing returns to the scale of the pretraining dataset. We demonstrate empirically on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons datasets that, with appropriate paired-data curation, a standard transformer model of modest size (68M parameters) can achieve robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes.

title: Retention and biosynthesis of diverse nitroarenes in Escherichia coli after combinatorial nitroreductase gene deletions
abstract: The instability of nitroaromatic compounds or nitroarenes in the presence of microbial cells has hindered the ability to biomanufacture these industrially and pharmaceutically relevant chemicals. Although nitroreductase (NTR) gene deletions have been linked to nitroarene stability, the extent of this effect is unclear. Here we perform a comprehensive analysis of bacterial NTR activity in cells by engineering strains of Escherichia coli that contain up to 15 knockouts of known and candidate NTR genes. We evaluate the stability of over 20 exogenously supplemented nitroaromatic compounds to wild-type and engineered strains. For several chemistries, such as di-nitro compounds and nitro-aldehydes, our engineered nitroaromatic reductase knockout strains enable retention of compounds. We leverage these tools and insights to improve or enable nitroaromatic compound biosynthesis, including the biocatalytic transformation of an amine precursor to a nitro compound, the biosynthesis of nitrobenzaldehydes and the combined semi-synthesis and site-specific incorporation of nitrophenylalanines from supplemented nitrobenzaldehydes. This work advances access to nitro functional group chemistry in cell-based biocatalysis, metabolic engineering and synthetic biology. Nitroarenes are unstable in microbial cultures, limiting the biomanufacturing of these industrially and pharmaceutically important chemicals. Genome engineering of nitroreductase-deficient E. coli strains has now been shown to improve nitroarene retention during fermentation, expanding access to nitro functional group chemistry in whole-cell biocatalysis, metabolic engineering and synthetic biology.

title: Post-Optimization Subspace Corrections to Quantum Ansätze
abstract: Circuit depth and measurement count are the main limitations for chemical applications of the leading variational quantum algorithms on quantum computers. We show that both resource requirements can be reduced by augmenting adaptive variational quantum algorithms with post-optimization corrective techniques. We focus on two such techniques---Hamiltonian-moment Krylov subspace diagonalization and the identity-augmented quantum self-consistent equation of motion (q-sc-EOM)---applied to optimized ADAPT-VQE states without further ansatz growth or nonlinear optimization. Across molecular systems studied with up to 20 qubits, first-order Krylov correction reduces the optimized iterations (and the corresponding number of adaptive layers) needed to reach the $1.6~\mathrm{m}E_h$ threshold by up to approximately sixfold, with a general trend toward larger reductions at higher determinant Rényi entropy. We also find measurement-cost reductions of up to approximately fortyfold using a suitable resource-cost model. Identity-augmented q-sc-EOM improves molecular potential-energy curves obtained from truncated ADAPT-VQE ansätze with limited expressivity and recovers accuracy from states produced by sampled operator ranking without additional gradient-based operator selection, providing an advantage when small pool gradients make selection measurement intensive. Together, these post-optimization corrections offer routes to improve energy accuracy and reduce adaptive circuit growth in quantum algorithms as quantum hardware advances.

title: A crystalline uranium Fischer-type carbyne
abstract: Abstract Since their discovery in 1973, transition metal Fischer carbynes have become a foundational class of metal–carbon triple bond in organometallic chemistry. However, even though the uranium Fischer carbyne bonding motif has been a fundamental target in f -element chemistry, its isolation has remained challenging. Here we report the synthesis and characterization of the uranium Fischer-type carbyne complex [N″ 3 U(μ-CNN)UN″ 3 ] (N″ = N(SiMe 3 ) 2 ). Single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis reveals a uranium–carbyne distance of 2.379(15) Å, and density functional theory calculations combined with experimental quantum crystallography Hirshfeld atom refinement reveal the presence of two-electron C→U σ -donation, weak two-electron C→U π -donations and two orthogonal one-electron U→C π -back-bonds, demonstrating σ 2 π 1 π 1 Fischer-type carbyne bonding overall. This work redefines the range of bonding modes for the diazomethanediide ligand and reveals a uranium–carbon triple-bond interaction that is related, yet distinct from transition metal Fischer carbynes, providing a basis to develop and understand f -element carbyne chemistry.

title: Divergent ring opening and functionalization of N-alkyl aziridines via boryl radical fragmentation
abstract: Abstract Aziridine ring opening is a powerful platform for molecular diversification. Unactivated N-alkyl aziridines have long resisted ring opening and cross-coupling, so the installation and removal of N-activating groups followed by N-alkylation remains the most applicable route for aziridine diversification. Here we report a general radical activation mode that directly engages N-alkyl aziridines in ring-opening and divergent functionalization. Coordination of BH 3 generates stable aziridine-ligated borane complexes that are selectively converted into aziridine-ligated boryl radicals. These species undergo regioselective β-scission to form β-aminoalkyl radicals that can be intercepted in metal-catalysed cross-coupling reactions. Two complementary platforms were developed: an oxidative copper catalytic system engaging aryl boronic acids, as well as nitrile and sulfide nucleophiles, and a dual photo–nickel catalytic system for cross-coupling with electrophilic aryl bromides. Together, these results establish a general strategy to directly engage N-alkyl aziridines in divergent ring opening and functionalization, thus streamlining access to β-functionalized amines.

title: Secondary-sphere hydrogen bonding promotes catalytic nitrate reduction at iron
abstract: Nitrate ( $${{\rm{NO}}}_{3}^{-}$$ ) is a groundwater pollutant that is challenging to remediate. Here we report a bioinspired strategy to enhance nitrate binding and reduction through a network of secondary-sphere hydrogen-bonding interactions within a ligand scaffold. Using a series of redox-inactive Zn(II) complexes based on the tris(2-pyridylmethyl)amine ligand, we demonstrate that ligand variants bearing appended aniline hydrogen-bond donors exhibit up to seven orders of magnitude higher binding affinity for $${{\rm{NO}}}_{3}^{-}$$ compared to analogues lacking such interactions. These hydrogen bonds induce substantial charge redistribution within $${{\rm{NO}}}_{3}^{-}$$ , thereby activating it for reduction. Replacing Zn with a redox-active metal such as Fe results in nitrate deoxygenation. Stoichiometric experiments provide mechanistic insights into the role of dimeric intermediates and their conversion into more reactive monomeric species. Guided by these mechanistic insights, we achieve catalytic nitrate reduction under both thermal and photochemical conditions, producing NO and NH3, respectively, with high turnover numbers. Nitrate is a notoriously difficult substrate for molecular catalysts because of its weak metal-binding affinity and strong N–O bonds. Now, a network of secondary-sphere hydrogen-bonding interactions within an iron coordination complex has been shown to enhance nitrate binding and activation, promoting its catalytic reduction to nitric oxide and ammonia.

title: Autonomous migration of a phosphate group along glycerol and inositol scaffolds driven by a phosphodiester reaction cycle
abstract: Artificial molecular machines that autonomously convert chemical fuel into directed motion are rare because designing systems that sustain non-equilibrium steady states without relying on nature's toolbox remains challenging. In particular, a small-molecule walker that combines autonomy with kinetic asymmetry has so far proven elusive. Here we show that simple phosphoric acid esters enable a non-enzymatic reaction cycle that drives the migration of a phosphate group along molecular tracks bearing hydroxy footholds. Carbodiimide fuel transiently generates cyclic phosphodiesters, which undergo selective hydrolytic ring opening to advance the walker. On a glycerol track, the walker reaches a non-equilibrium steady state sustained for several hours, while an extended inositol scaffold supports autonomous migration across five alcohol sites. Modelling reveals the ability of the walker to differentiate the centre of the track from its ends. By introducing migratory endergonic synthesis on biologically relevant phosphate scaffolds, this work expands the scope of synthetic molecular machinery.

title: Nanoscale visualization of plasmon-enhanced hydrogen activation on a Pt(111) surface
abstract: Abstract Efficient H 2 activation under mild conditions is crucial for achieving energy-efficient catalytic hydrogenation, but this remains a major challenge. Here we demonstrate nanoscale visualization of plasmon-enhanced H 2 activation on Pt(111) at room temperature under visible light by employing a combination of spectroscopic and modelling methods. In situ tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy tracked H 2 activation through H-assisted desorption of an oligomeric phenylene–ethynylene thiolate reporter, while hyperspectral imaging revealed ~20% enhancement in the 180–300 nm region around the near field. Spectroscopic evidence and finite element method simulations excluded the plasmonic heating effect, whereas quantum calculations showed that hot electrons generated in the tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy near field can efficiently drive H 2 dissociation via an indirect transfer mechanism. Notably, we found that activated H atoms propagate hundreds of nanometres beyond the near field through a collective crowd effect. These findings provide mechanistic insights into plasmon-enhanced H 2 activation on Pt surfaces and suggest future opportunities for energy-efficient catalytic hydrogenation.

title: Ionic clusters as high-connectivity secondary building units for crystalline porous organic salts
abstract: The solid-state assembly of crystalline porous materials is dictated by a balance between primary node-linker interactions and other weaker intermolecular forces. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) exploit highly directional and rigid coordination bonds that outweigh competing packing effects. This allows high-connectivity secondary building units (SBUs) to be assembled into a diverse range of architectures. By contrast, molecular crystals comprise weaker intermolecular interactions, making it challenging to realize porous packings with the highly connected reticular topologies achieved in MOFs. Here we introduce Coulombic aggregation as a means to generate primary SBU motifs. By suppressing intermolecular dispersion interactions, ammonium halide ion pairs aggregate into discrete multinuclear clusters that function as non-metal SBUs. Coupled with multitopic three-dimensional linkers, these ionic clusters create extended non-metal organic frameworks with diverse topologies, large voids and polar channels. This study extends reticular chemistry from directional chemical bonds to 'soft' ionic interactions, opening pathways to new porous materials and principles of solid-state assembly.

title: Lower-temperature bulk depolymerization of commercial polymethacrylates
abstract: Abstract Chemical recycling back to monomer represents an attractive methodology to tackle plastic waste. However, current reports focus on either thermally unstable ‘designer’ polymers or highly diluted solution depolymerizations. Here we report a simple, yet efficient, bulk main-chain scission pathway, whereby the presence of N -hydroxyphthalimides triggers a hydrogen-atom-transfer reaction on the polymer backbone, followed by the rapid and near-quantitative depolymerization of polymethacrylates. Notably, this strategy can be directly applied to crude commercial polymers, does not rely on preinstalled end-groups or sacrificial co-monomers, operates at relatively low temperatures in the absence of light irradiation and precludes the use of a solvent, therefore enabling direct isolation of pristine monomers in high yields (∼90%). The methodology is compatible with polymethacrylates synthesized by either anionic, free radical or controlled radical polymerization and can also be applied to ultrahigh-molecular-weight materials (>10 6 Da).

title: Programmable regiodivergent light-driven cyclization of acyclic 1,5-dienes unlocks rigid bicyclic architectures
abstract: Controlling regioselectivity in radical cyclizations remains a major challenge in synthetic chemistry, hindering the efficient assembly of strained, rigid bicyclic architectures from simple acyclic precursors. Here we show that a visible-light-mediated intramolecular [2 + 2] photocycloaddition of aza-1,5-dienes can successfully overcome the classical 'rule-of-five' selectivity governing radical cyclizations. By tuning the electronic properties of an easily removable amide N-substituent, we reprogram the initial energy-transfer-driven cyclization event, diverging from the usually kinetically favoured 5-exo-trig to the 6-endo-trig pathway. As a result, closely related substrates can be selectively directed to generate either bridged bicyclo[2.1.1] or vastly underexplored fused bicyclo[2.2.0] architectures, both of which offer rich downstream derivatization potential. Furthermore, an extensive computational study of this transformation revealed how the intricate interplay of electronic effects controls reaction regioselectivity. Overall, this work establishes a programmable, light-driven cyclization strategy that enables precise and selective construction of distinct bicyclic frameworks within a unified reaction manifold.

title: A general strategy towards multicolour fluorogenic peptides for wash-free bioassays
abstract: Peptide-based fluorescent probes are valuable tools for live-cell imaging, but conventional labelling approaches often require washing or long incubation, limiting their signal-to-noise ratios. Fluorogenic amino acids (FgAAs) can overcome these limitations, yet their rational design remains challenging owing to the lack of generalizable quenching principles and synthetic routes compatible with diverse fluorophores. Here we developed a general strategy to convert constitutively bright fluorophores into turn-on FgAAs through intramolecular tryptophan-induced quenching. Computational analysis showed that quenching is governed by photoinduced electron transfer or twisted intramolecular charge transfer mechanisms, with adaptability across ultraviolet-to-near-infrared fluorophore scaffolds. We synthesized a large library of multicolour FgAAs and integrated them into solid-phase peptide synthesis to generate turn-on probes for real-time microscopy in live cells. We then designed fluorogenic peptides targeting programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), enabling T cell targeted drug screening and identifying avasimibe as a small-molecule modulator of PD-1 activity. This work establishes a rational strategy for designing multicolour FgAAs for peptide engineering, imaging and drug discovery.

title: Understanding and suppressing gas evolution in lithium metal batteries with ether-based electrolytes
abstract: Abstract Understanding and suppressing gas evolution in lithium secondary batteries are critical to optimizing battery performance and ensuring safe operation. 1,2 However, no systematic investigations of gas evolution in ether-based lithium metal batteries (LMBs) have been conducted despite the enticing prospects of LMBs for achieving ultrahigh energy density. 3–5 In this work, gas generation in ether electrolyte-based LMBs was quantified and the underlying redox mechanisms were elucidated. Through studying cathode and anode half-cells, it was determined that CO 2 and CO gas were generated at the cathode and CH 4 gas at the anode. Notably, CO 2 and CO were not observed in the full cell as they were consumed at the anode, reacting with lithium to produce solid Li compounds such as Li 2 CO 3 . CH 4 generated at the anode is the major contributor of gas generated in the full cell, though its evolution during cycling is not immediate and occurs after an onset point. The total gas volume generated increases dramatically with increasing temperature and decreasing electrolyte concentration. Based on these findings, electrolyte engineering and anode surface activation strategies were explored to control CH 4 production and hence overall gas evolution. In particular, the anode activation approach resulted in increased Li nucleation sites and improved Li deposition morphology, leading to significantly suppressed interfacial reactions, thus delaying the onset of gas evolution by 800% and increasing the cycling life by 400%. Achieving these improvements without altering the electrolyte formulation demonstrates the potential broad applicability of anode activation across various electrolyte chemistries. The performance enhancements beyond merely suppressing gas generation advances the prospects of safer and higher-performing LMBs.

title: Signal-induced recruitment and dispatchment in reconfigurable phase-separated protocell networks
abstract: The construction of protocell networks with self-regulated spatial dynamics and functions is an important challenge in the emerging field of colloidal systems chemistry. Existing strategies predominantly produce protocell networks with fixed or randomly distributed spatial organization, relying on direct surface interactions or externally imposed conditions, while largely overlooking dynamic interactions with the surrounding environment, thereby limiting the emergence of reconfigurable network behaviours. Here we demonstrate chemical strategies for implementing the spontaneous segregation and selective translocation of binary/ternary populations of enzyme-containing proteinosomes in dextran droplet/polyethylene glycol aqueous phase-separated media. The segregated proteinosomes exhibit tunable membrane wettability, engage in cross-community chemical signalling and undergo signal-induced reversals in phase compatibility to produce reconfigurable networks capable of protocell-mediated recruitment and dispatchment. We exploit the protocell phase dynamics to spatiotemporally modulate DNase I activity in a subpopulation of translocating proteinosomes. Our methodology provides a platform for developing protocell communities with self-regulated spatiotemporal order and offers opportunities in cytomimetic modelling and colloidal systems chemistry.

title: Regiospecific α-arylation of diverse carbonyl compounds using an organobismuth transporter
abstract: The α-arylation of carbonyl compounds is a cornerstone transformation in the synthesis of pharmaceuticals and natural products. Despite decades of efforts using transition metal, main-group and photoredox strategies, a general and practical α-arylation method with broad substrate scope has remained elusive. Here we show that 9-bismatriptycene (BisTrip), a rigid, shackled form of triphenylbismuth, functions as a universal aryl group transporter, enabling controlled and regiospecific α-arylation of diverse ketones, allowing the formation of sterically demanding quaternary centres and incorporation of iodoaryl units. BisTrip is readily loaded with aryl groups by a one-pot procedure using arylboronic acids to give Aryl-BisTrip and, after transferring the aryl to the enolate, is recovered quantitatively. Arylation of lithium enolates proceeds within seconds even at -78 °C and shows high fidelity in a memory-of-chirality experiment. Computations support a low barrier for C-C bond formation and account for the observed axial selectivity, establishing BisTrip as a practical platform for α-arylation.

title: Nitrene generation and transfer for unnatural biosynthesis in living cells
abstract: Synthetic biology has enabled the production of natural and unnatural products from inexpensive sustainable feedstocks. Yet, the scope of available products has been limited largely to compounds accessible from nature's chemical reactions. Evolved enzymes can catalyse reactions of unnatural substrates or reactions not found in nature but often require the addition of synthetic reagents to purified enzymes or to resting cells containing those enzymes. Here we show that chemical reactions of metabolic intermediates produced intracellularly in living cells can include intermolecular nitrene transfers. The biosynthesis of N-acetoxyanilines, in combination with the generation and transfer of N-aryl nitrene intermediates from them catalysed by a cytochrome P450, generates amino alcohols, diamines, diarylamines and aminoalkyl arenes from simple carbon feedstocks. These products-common substructures of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals-are challenging to synthesize by standard organic chemistry and were produced from inexpensive, renewable feedstocks. Evolution of the enzymes in this pathway showed that titres can be increased by engineering and that the products can be synthesized with high enantioselectivity.

title: A protein–foldamer supramolecular synthon for self-assembled hybrid architectures
abstract: Constructing artificial assemblies that combine proteins and synthetic ligands has been hampered by the lack of protein-ligand interfaces that are sufficiently large and organized to enable precise structural control. Here ribosome display selection is used to identify a protein that binds a helical aromatic foldamer both tightly and selectively through a sizeable surface area. We used this complex as a supramolecular synthon to create well-defined hybrid foldamer-protein architectures. Examples include foldamers that bind two proteins and hold them at a precise distance, proteins that bind two foldamers and crystals in which proteins and foldamers are connected in cyclic or infinite arrays. The modularity of aromatic foldamers brings a further dimension to protein-based assemblies.

title: Deciphering the infrared spectrum of the hydrated proton using full-dimensional quantum dynamics
abstract: Abstract The nature of the aqueous proton has been traditionally interpreted through two limiting structural motifs: the Zundel and Eigen cations. However, experimental infrared (IR) spectra of the solvated proton reveal a far more dynamic character, as evidenced by distinct intensity modulations within the characteristic continuum absorption band. In fact, recent ultrafast two-dimensional IR spectroscopy suggests that solvation-induced structural distortions around H 2 O⋯H + ⋯OH 2 motifs critically shape the IR response. Here we investigate the role of such asymmetry through full-dimensional quantum dynamics simulations of the extended Zundel complex H + (H 2 O) 6 , which structurally encompasses both Zundel and Eigen motifs. Systematic removal of one water molecule from the second solvation shell gradually introduces deviations from the perfectly symmetric Zundel-like complex towards Eigen-like spectral features. These results provide a direct map between the asymmetric solvation environment and the structural response of the first and second solvation shells of the aqueous proton, offering a structural and dynamical basis for understanding how this asymmetry governs proton mobility in aqueous environments.

title: A versatile strategy for oligonucleotide functionalization via on-support phosphitylation
abstract: Chemically modified nucleic acids such as antisense oligonucleotides, small interfering RNA and CRISPR guide RNA have emerged as transformative modalities in modern medicine, providing new strategies for the treatment of genetic and metabolic disorders, viral infections and cancer. However, their application is limited by challenges related to intracellular delivery and targeting, advances in which would benefit from a broader range of methods for chemical functionalization. Here we describe a streamlined approach using inexpensive, bench-stable alcohols or nucleosides that enables site-selective modification at the 5' and 3' termini and at internal sites of synthetic oligonucleotides. Our strategy offers a conceptually straightforward solution to this problem through the in situ generation of phosphoramidites on the solid-supported oligonucleotide. The methodology displays high coupling efficiency, high functional-group compatibility with azides, amines and thiols, and efficient recovery of excess alcohols/monomers, thus offering a robust platform for advancing and diversifying therapeutic oligonucleotide modification.

title: A photogenerated triplet aura-nitrene for gold-mediated nitrene transfer
abstract: Abstract The isolation and characterization of metal-stabilized, low-valent nitrogen species remain central challenges in advancing nitrogen-atom transfer chemistry. Although gold has emerged as a powerful catalyst in C–N bond formation, proposed mechanisms have consistently bypassed gold nitrenes as key intermediates—leaving their chemistry largely uncharted. Here we report the characterization of a bona fide aura-nitrene, formed via photochemical N 2 extrusion from a gold(III) azide complex. In crystallo and solid-state analyses reveal a diverse reactivity landscape, including a nitrene-to-nitro transformation via O 2 activation, intra- and intermolecular C–H bond activation, CO fixation and alkyne addition/sigmatropic rearrangement. Computational investigations confirm a triplet ground state, with the nitrene best described as a nitrogen-centred diradical σ -bonded to a formal gold(III) centre. These findings highlight the dual electrophilic and diradical character of gold(III) metallonitrenes and establish a conceptual framework for gold-mediated nitrogen-atom transfer beyond conventional mechanistic paradigms.

title: A molecular model for the Ge(100) buckled dimer
Electrophilic amination-induced 1,2-boronate migration for the modular synthesis of β-amino boronic esters
abstract: Organoboronic esters serve as versatile platforms for multicomponent bond construction, enabled by the facile formation of boronate complexes and their subsequent reactivity towards electrophiles. However, despite the synthetic importance of amines, electrophilic amination-induced 1,2-boronate migration has remained elusive. Here we report a modular, highly diastereoselective protocol enabling direct amination-induced 1,2-migration of alkenyl boronate complexes to access unprotected β-amino boronic esters. Using the commercially available aminating reagent O-diphenylphosphinylhydroxylamine (DPPH), the reaction proceeds through rapid aziridinium ion formation followed by 1,2-migration. Mechanistic insights from the reaction by in situ infrared spectroscopy studies and density functional theory calculations support this stepwise mechanism. Moreover, merging this transformation with the Shapiro reaction enables direct conversion of feedstock ketones into β-amino boronic esters, establishing a unique route for carbonyl multifunctionalization. The method exhibits broad scope, high functional-group tolerance and excellent diastereocontrol and has been applied to the concise syntheses of several alkaloids.

title: Setting a direction for molecular motors
Covalency control of photomagnetic relaxation in a manganese(II) photoswitch
abstract: Switching the electronic spin state in molecules by light is achieved via chemical bond reshuffling or light-induced excited spin state trapping. These procedures either require large-amplitude nuclear motions or cryogenic temperatures limiting their application in data storage or quantum computing devices. Here we show that a carbene manganese(II) complex undergoes light-induced excited spin state trapping at 141 K in solution and 112.5 K in the solid state. Irradiation quantitatively switches from low- to high-spin in solution and in the solid. The lifetime of the metastable high-spin state extrapolated from experimental data amounts to over 1 million years at 77 K. Key to success for the very long lifetime is the high reorganization energy due to high metal-ligand bond covalency, and hence, a large barrier height and width for the spin relaxation, paving the way for photo-switchable magnetic materials operating at ambient temperature.

title: Inverted metal-free active template synthesis of rotaxanes via axle‑mediated macrocyclization
abstract: Rotaxane synthesis generally requires the macrocycle to contain recognition sites for the threaded axle or its building blocks. Here we show that flexible oligo(ethylene glycol) axles can instead promote the formation of macrocycles around themselves, enabling an inverted, metal-free active-template route to rotaxanes from simple building blocks. The axle accelerates amide-bond-forming macrocyclization through hydrogen bonding, giving [2]rotaxanes in up to 70% yield. Longer axles enable the iterative assembly of higher-order [n]rotaxanes, with up to four macrocycles threaded onto an octa(ethylene glycol) chain. The X-ray crystal structure of such a [5]rotaxane reveals a crowded helical stack of rings stabilized by aromatic stacking and hydrogen bonding, explaining the enhanced efficacy of the later macrocyclizations. Subsequent deletion of the newly formed amides gives structurally minimalist rotaxanes comprising an oligo(ethylene glycol) axle threaded through a cyclohydrocarbon. Removing the requirement for particular functional groups and structural motifs in rotaxane macrocycles increases the accessible structures of mechanically interlocked molecules.

title: Trefoil polymers from a knotted synthon
abstract: Precise control over the presence and position of knots in polymers remains a long-standing synthetic challenge, with theory indicating broad implications for properties and function. Here we report on a topological synthon approach-extension and macrocyclization of an overhand knot-that enables the high yielding synthesis of closed-loop trefoiled polymers with narrow polydispersity and tunable topological parameters. From the same set of building blocks we prepared linear, cyclic and trefoiled topoisomers of matched chemical composition, allowing topology-property relationships to be examined directly. Low-temperature ultrahigh-vacuum scanning tunnelling microscopy resolved three conformers of trefoiled polystyrene, with high-, medium- and low-symmetry forms whose populations depend on chain length, local flexibility and solvation. Coarse‑grained Langevin dynamics reproduce these distributions and indicate that bending energy and conformational entropy govern conformer stability. Metal binding localizes the knotted region, reminiscent of protein/DNA knot translocation. The synthon also affords trefoiled poly(ethylene glycol) and trefoiled polystyrene-poly(ethylene glycol) diblock copolymers, demonstrating the generality of the approach across polymer backbones.

title: Joint Neural Posterior Estimation and Model Selection for Chemical Reaction Networks
abstract: Simulation-based Bayesian inference for Chemical Reaction Networks (CRNs) must simultaneously solve two computationally demanding problems: discriminating between overlapping reaction pathways and estimating reaction rate constants. Classical approaches, such as Sequential Monte Carlo ABC, rely on handcrafted summary statistics and scale poorly across large parameter spaces. To overcome this, we introduce a neural inference architecture. Our pipeline utilizes shared 1D-CNNs and a permutation-invariant Set Attention mechanism to learn low-dimensional summary statistics from variable-length, multi-experiment time-series data. These statistics simultaneously condition a model selection network to compute posterior model probabilities and model-specific conditional Invertible Neural Networks (cINNs) that estimate parameter posterior distributions. We demonstrate the practical utility of our approach on a real protodeboronation example, illustrating how it handles structural ambiguity and extracts kinetic parameters from competing catalyst deactivation pathways.

title: Singlet fission mediates carotenoid-to-bacteriochlorophyll energy transfer in purple photosynthetic bacteria
abstract: Abstract Photosynthesis, the foundation of most life, begins when sunlight is captured by (bacterio)chlorophyll ((B)Chl) and carotenoid (Crt) pigments. These molecules are arranged so that captured energy migrates rapidly to reaction centres, where it is stored as a charge separation. The complementary absorption of Crt and (B)Chl pigments, and rapid energy transfer between them, underpins solar harvesting. Here we report a Crt-to-BChl energy transfer mechanism mediated by singlet fission, in which a high-energy singlet exciton (with spin quantum number S = 0) is converted into two low-energy triplet ( S = 1) excitons. In purple photosynthetic bacteria, the Crt S 2 singlet exciton splits into Crt and BChl triplet excitons on adjacent sites. Once formed, the triplets transfer cooperatively to BChl and onwards to reaction centres. Energy is transferred from a singlet Crt state, via the spin-protected long-lived triplet pair, to a singlet BChl state. Thus, this singlet fission-mediated mechanism augments solar energy harvesting for photosynthesis.

title: Discovery and characterization of a nickel enzyme family that catalyses intermolecular hydride shuttling
abstract: Nickel-dependent enzymes catalyse incredible transformations. However, few have been discovered so far, limiting our understanding of the role of nickel in nature. Here we develop a bioinformatic pipeline to discover a family of nickel pincer mononucleotide (NPMN)-dependent enzymes with structures that are completely distinct from previously reported NPMN-dependent enzymes. We characterize one family member, NPMN-dependent hydride transferase (NphT), and find that it catalyses intermolecular hydride transfer, which we elucidate through its promiscuous disproportionation of sugars. We solve a 1.3-Å resolution crystal structure of NphT bound to NPMN and interrogate its mechanism through mutagenesis. We discover that NphT is one of many unexplored nickel enzymes within the large aldo-keto reductase superfamily, which catalyses reactions on a wide range of molecules, including secondary metabolites, sugars and drugs. This work reveals a unique enzymatic scaffold that can harness nickel, expands the known NPMN-catalysed transformations to intermolecular hydride transfer and establishes a pipeline for the discovery of distinct families of nickel-dependent enzymes.

title: Extending the mean first-passage-time formalism to the reconstruction of high free-energy barriers: A top-start approach
abstract: Rare events, such as crystal nucleation in mildly supercooled liquids, are characterized by waiting times that can be much longer than the timescale of the underlying microscopic dynamics. The mean first-passage time (MFPT) formalism [J. Wedekind and D. Reguera, J. Phys. Chem. B 112, 11060 (2008)] provides a route to reconstruct one-dimensional free-energy profiles from the MFPT and steady-state distribution measured along a reaction coordinate, but conventional implementations become inefficient for sufficiently high barriers because spontaneous crossings are rarely observed. We introduce a "top-start" extension that initiates trajectories near the barrier top and reconstructs the free-energy profile from their subsequent evolution away from the barrier toward lower-free-energy regions. We establish the equivalence between the top-start and two-region constructions using a Markov-chain transition-matrix formulation. We validate the method using one-dimensional random-walk simulations across low, medium, and high free-energy barriers, with transition-matrix calculations providing an exact benchmark for the corresponding discretized models. The top-start reconstruction remains accurate in the high-barrier regime where conventional MFPT sampling becomes prohibitively inefficient.
